title: Why the F1 driver market might produce one last twist
excerpt:
On paper, the news Racing Bulls will keep both Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad for next season leaves just one spot to be confirmed, but there's still the possibility of a change in one other seat on the grid...

So what's up for grabs in that one spot yet to be confirmed?

A seat at American squad Haas. Ollie Bearman is the incumbent and is going to be in it next year – they just haven't nailed down the details of the contract.

The Briton and Ferrari junior is in his second full season with Haas and currently sits in 13th place in the drivers' standings on 23 points.

He's levelled up in his second campaign, both in terms of Qualifying pace and racecraft – with the 21-year-old pulling off some particularly impressive overtakes.

Haas certainly want to keep him – so it's just a case of his management, Haas boss Ayao Komatsu and Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur coming to an agreement.

While it is a no-brainer for all parties to continue, the terms of the deal are important as Bearman will know that if Lewis Hamilton keeps delivering, he won't be leaving Ferrari anytime soon and that means there's no space for the Briton to move up.

And while Haas is a great place to be for Bearman for now – and his full focus is taking the team forward and helping them achieve the first podium in their history – he also knows he can't stay there forever if he wants to progress his career.

Watch this space, but it's certainly a case of when, not if, a deal is done for 2027.

'We see huge potential' – Komatsu on choosing Camara for Haas

Okay, that finalises the grid – so what's this about a possible change?

Well, this is where we turn our attention to Cadillac. When Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas signed with the newcomers ahead of this campaign, they both agreed multi-year deals.

These multi-year deals had options which needed triggering to confirm the second season in 2027.

Ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix, Cadillac announced Perez had signed an extended deal keeping him at the team until at least the end of 2029.

A subsequent announcement about Bottas has yet to be released, with the team's American reserve driver Colton Herta linked with the seat that would offer him his F1 debut.

Herta has struggled in F2 and sits 19th in the standings, but the 26-year-old has impressed when behind the wheel of a Cadillac in FP1 sessions and the American team are keen to run an American driver on merit.

By taking part in the opening practice session in Brazil, Herta secured the final point needed for his Super Licence, clearing the way for a potential F1 drive.

Cadillac now have to decide whether they want to give him a debut next year or stick with 37-year-old 10-time Grand Prix winner Bottas alongside Perez.

What about one-time Grand Prix winner Esteban Ocon?

Given Haas are set to sign Bearman and Cadillac will have Bottas or Herta, it means there is no space on the grid for Ocon, who made his F1 debut back in 2016.

Earlier this month, Haas announced that Ocon would not complete the season with the team, which he was set to leave at the end of the year anyway.

Ocon – who has won one Grand Prix, taken four podiums and scored 490 points in 198 starts – has unfinished business with F1 and wants to find a way back in.

Initially, that will have to be a reserve role at best and with his experience in F1, it's believed he does have options for 2027.

title: Tsolov to serve as Red Bull and Racing Bulls reserve driver
excerpt:
Red Bull and Racing Bulls have confirmed that Formula 2 racer Nikola Tsolov will serve as their shared reserve driver for the 2027 season.

The announcement follows the news that Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will continue to form Racing Bulls’ driver line-up for another year, ending speculation that Tsolov could be promoted to a full-time seat.

Instead, the Bulgarian will join both the Faenza-based outfit and sister team Red Bull in a reserve capacity, which means he will be on standby to race if required, develop the car through simulator work, and get the opportunity to drive in further FP1 sessions – having previously impressed during his first outing in Mexico City – and Testing of Previous Cars (TPC).

The move follows Tsolov's progression through the junior categories, having finished runner-up in the 2025 Formula 3 championship before stepping up to F2, where he remains in title contention with two rounds remaining.

Tsolov said: “I’m incredibly happy and grateful to Red Bull for giving me this opportunity. Since joining the Junior Team, I’ve received amazing support and have developed so much, both as a driver and as a person. My career has progressed incredibly quickly, and I owe a lot to everyone who has believed in me and helped me get to this point.

“My ambition is clear: I want to become an F1 driver. Having the opportunity to spend next year preparing for that next step is incredibly exciting.

“I’m confident that with the Team’s support and experience, I’ll have the best possible preparation to make sure I’m fully ready to take the next step onto the F1 grid when the time comes.

“I know there is still a lot to learn, but I’m ready to work hard, make the most of every opportunity and give everything I have to the Team. For now, my immediate focus is on finishing the F2 season as strongly as possible.”

CEO and Red Bull Team Principal Laurent Mekies added: “Nikola is an exceptionally talented young driver, and we have been hugely impressed by his development and performances over the past few years.

“To fight for the Championship in F3 and now challenge for the F2 title in his first full season says a great deal about his ability and determination. What has impressed us just as much is his maturity, his approach to racing and his willingness to keep learning and improving.

“We have enormous belief in Nikola’s potential and see him as a driver with a very exciting future in F1. This appointment reflects our confidence in him and our commitment to his continued development. Our focus in 2027 will be on giving him the experience, tools and support he needs to be ready to race in F1 next.

“For now, Nikola still has an important job to finish in F2. We wish him every success in the final two rounds and will be supporting him all the way as he fights for the Championship.”

title: Russell launches new karting academy for young racers
excerpt:
George Russell has revealed the creation of his own karting academy, which will seek to find “hidden stars” and provide support to help them progress in motorsport when it officially launches in 2027.

The Mercedes driver teased the announcement earlier this week as he praised karting for teaching him “the fundamentals of racing” and making him the competitor he is now, adding his ambition to “give back to a sport that gave me so much”.

The GR63 Academy will begin with open-access qualifiers at Silverstone in December, with 80 young drivers progressing to a shoot-out before 25 are selected for the 2027 championship.

“So proud to introduce you all to the GR63 Academy,” Russell shared on social media. “Karting is where it all started for me and has played a crucial role in my career. I also know how hard it is for talented young drivers to get that first opportunity, especially when budgets are tight.

“With the GR63 Academy, I want to give something back to my sport by finding those hidden stars and giving them the support and guidance they need to reach their potential.

“Following the first two rounds at Silverstone, I’ll identify 25 kids to take part in the GR63 Academy in 2027. Thank you to Silverstone and the BRDC for helping make this happen.”

The academy's official website outlines the selection process, beginning with Arrive & Drive Qualifiers in December. Children aged eight or nine can participate for £25 per qualifying session.

The 80 fastest drivers will advance to a shoot-out at the end of January, with 25 selected to compete in the GR63 Championship – a fully funded, eight-round series held across different circuit configurations at Kart Silverstone.

Equipped with a full set of Russell’s signature vibrant blue kit, they will battle to finish in the top five, which will earn them a spot in the final shoot-out. There, the remaining youngsters will be assessed on “talent, lap times, fitness, race craft and media skills”, with the winner receiving a fully-funded kart season in 2028.

Russell believes the initiative could help uncover F1's next generation of talent by providing a more accessible route into competitive karting.

title: Why Racing Bulls stuck with Lawson and Lindblad
excerpt:
There'll be no change in Racing Bulls' line-up for next season, with Arvid Lindblad's encouraging rookie year and a sensational campaign from Liam Lawson enough to secure their respective seats.

Why did Lindblad get the nod?

Lindblad has caught the eye this year, kicking off life in F1 with points on debut in Australia and going on a run of 10 points finishes in 11 Grands Prix weekends midway through the year.

His progression both on and off track has been solid through the year, with the team impressed with his feedback, calmness under pressure and natural speed.

Though the last four events have been point-less for the 19-year-old, there was still underlying growth in his performances, including a strong drive from 18th to 11th last time out in Brazil.

It's believed that Red Bull and Racing Bulls have been convinced for some time that Lindblad, who sits 11th in the Drivers' Standings, deserved another year.

What was the challenge with the second seat?

The second seat was less certain because even if Lawson was enjoying the best season of his career by quite some distance, Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov was making waves in F2.

Lawson has looked like a driver reborn at Racing Bulls, following his demotion from Red Bull after just two races at the start of 2025, with his performance in 2026 particularly impressive.

The 24-year-old has scored points in 15 of the 20 Grands Prix this year (two of those were when he subbed in at Red Bull) - as well as taking points in three Sprints where only the top eight score.

That form puts him best of the rest and top of the midfield pack in P9 in the drivers' standings with a points tally of 89, more than double the tally of the next best driver Pierre Gasly.

However, with Tsolov leading the championship in F2 until the previous round when he was usurped by Ferrari junior and incoming full-time Haas driver Rafa Camara, Red Bull were considering promoting him.

With six victories in F2, Tsolov has well and truly been one to watch, and when he got behind the wheel of the Racing Bulls machine in FP1 at Mexico, he impressed the team with his speed and feedback.

Lawson and Lindblad to remain at Racing Bulls for 2027

That piled pressure on Lawson. Despite impressing during his three-race stint replacing the injured Isack Hadjar at Red Bull, a permanent return appears unlikely, strengthening the case for Racing Bulls to develop another potential Red Bull driver.

Racing Bulls Team Principal Alan Permane, who was recently handed a new contract that will keep him at the helm until at least the end of 2031, told me last year that he wants the team to be "an incubator for talent".

And so that's why Racing Bulls found themselves with a dilemma.

Why did they choose Lawson over Tsolov?

Ultimately, it came down to performance. Lawson's tally of 89 points has been crucial in the team establishing themselves in P5 in the Teams' Championship, 45 points clear of Alpine.

The Faenza-based team have never finished as high as fifth in their 20-year history, so Lawson's contribution to putting them on the path to making history played a big role.

Even with the pressure of Tsolov waiting in the wings, Lawson has absorbed it all and continued to deliver across the last triple header, following a ninth in Austin with a brace of seventh places.

That form - combined with his results across the rest of the year - is what Red Bull and Racing Bulls will have hoped to get from a driver in one of their cars.

His race craft has tightened up, he's cut out the mistakes - and he seems to have found a way to get the best out of himself more consistently across a race weekend.

The New Zealander works well with Lindblad and they felt that continuity and stability was the right move for 2027 as they look to build on their very strong campaign in 2026.

What does that mean for Tsolov?

The Bulgarian will have to wait a little longer, but it's believed it's a case of when, not if, he'll make the step up to Formula 1 with the Red Bull family.

The energy drinks firm rate him highly and he's progressing as they would expect. Having more time to prepare himself for a debut in Formula 1 can only be a good thing.

WATCH: FIA Formula 2 – Where F1 Stars Are Made

The team haven't confirmed what his role will look like going forward but it's likely they will make him a reserve driver to continue his integration with the team.

It's also likely that he will get more opportunities in FP1 - teams have to run a rookie in at least four FP1s per year - and some running in old-spec F1 machinery to continue to build his experience.

All this puts Racing Bulls in a very strong position. They have two drivers performing at a very high level and one driver readying himself for a step up.

It's exactly how they and Red Bull will have hoped their junior programme conveyor belt would work.

title: Lawson and Lindblad to remain at Racing Bulls for 2027
excerpt:
Racing Bulls have confirmed they will field an unchanged line-up of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad for the 2027 season, with both drivers extending their contracts with the team.

Lawson’s future at Racing Bulls has been the subject of speculation in recent months, with Red Bull Junior Nikola Tsolov emerging as a potential replacement and Team Principal Alan Permane repeatedly insisting that no final decision had been made.

Speaking a week after Tsolov made his FP1 debut for Racing Bulls, Permane explained that the team were “trying to apply a little bit of science” to make “the right decision”.

That has led to the New Zealander’s new deal, which also comes after his spectacular Sao Paulo Grand Prix weekend where he started third and wound up seventh, taking him to 89 points in the standings – more than the season total for Racing Bulls’ midfield rivals Alpine.

It marked his fourth seventh-place finish in five Grands Prix and strengthened Racing Bulls' grip on fifth in the Constructors' Championship. Should they retain that position, it would represent their best-ever result, dating back to their origins as Minardi.

Additionally, Lawson's team mate Lindblad has contributed a crucial 38 points to that goal and impressed with his consistency as a rookie, earning a sophomore campaign with Racing Bulls.

Lawson said: “I’m very happy to be continuing with Visa Cash App Racing Bulls next year. We’ve had a brilliant season together and the team has worked very hard to produce a fast car, which I’ve loved driving.

"It feels great to be part of a historic season for the team as we continue our fight for P5 in the Constructors' Championship. It's a testament to the hard work of everyone both at track, and back at the factory.

"I’m looking forward to carrying this moment forward with Arvid through to 2027; we’re building something super positive and I’m excited by what we can achieve together.”

Lindblad added: "I'm very happy to be continuing with Visa Cash App Racing Bulls in 2027. Looking back on my first season in Formula One, it's been a truly special year, full of new experiences and learnings since the very first pre-season test.

"I'd like to thank everyone at VCARB and Red Bull for their trust and support. I'm incredibly grateful to everyone in the team for their hard work, commitment and collaboration throughout the season, and for the strong relationships we've built along the way.

"I can't wait to get started next year, building on everything I've learned during my rookie season. It's set to be an exciting year, and I look forward to continuing to drive alongside Liam."

Team Principal Permane said: "We’re delighted to be continuing with Liam and Arvid for 2027. Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we’ve seen the progress they’ve made, both individually and as a pairing.

"I have no doubt that this is the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition. Together, we have a solid foundation to build on the progress made this year, continue pushing ourselves forward and take the next step towards achieving our ambitions in 2027."

The announcement leaves two uncertainties on the 2027 grid, with Haas yet to disclose news of a contract for Ollie Bearman, although both parties have expressed a desire to continue working together.

Over at Cadillac, Valtteri Bottas was signed to a multi-year deal, but an extension for his team mate Sergio Perez – as well as the completed mission to secure a Super Licence for test driver Colton Herta – have raised some question marks around his place on the grid next season.

title: Ricciardo reacts to his best career moments
excerpt:
Daniel Ricciardo brought an energy to F1 that the sport had never quite witnessed before, adding a sense of joy and humour that delighted both those in the paddock and at home. But more importantly, he was a determined, ruthless competitor who clinched eight Grand Prix victories across stints at Red Bull and McLaren.

Two years have passed since the Australian left the sport, so he recently took the time to relive his greatest highlights and offer unprecedented insight into his career in an exclusive interview…

Ricciardo’s first victory

In his first season with Red Bull, Ricciardo had stood on the podium twice before securing his maiden victory at the 2014 Canadian Grand Prix. Starting from sixth on the grid, he steadily worked his way up and benefitted from Lewis Hamilton’s retirement to bring himself into contention in the race’s final stages.

Decisive moves on Sergio Perez and Nico Rosberg over the last few laps sealed the win for Ricciardo, and all he could get out over the radio was a chuckle and “wow!”.

“I didn't really know what to say,” he explained. “I think it was such a young laugh of shock and joy. I mean, the first emotion is – I don't know, is nostalgia an emotion? It feels so familiar, but also so long ago. I'm also just very grateful to have been able to experience this feeling. That's the highest high in the sport. Beyond that is to win a World Championship.

“For many years, I didn't feel like my career was a success because the World Championship was something that I was so fixed on and believed in. But I think now looking back, I'm like, okay, this was pretty awesome to still be able to get these moments.”

When his maiden pole position led to heartbreak in Monaco

Ricciardo already had three victories under his belt when he took his long-awaited maiden pole position and established himself as something of a Monaco specialist.

“That was a good lap,” he summarised. “I remember that. That was a good car as well. Monaco is special. There was definitely a good chunk of my career that I felt like I had an edge in Monaco.

“I had two poles in three years there. It didn't feel like a big deal because I was so high on confidence and that belief in myself – not in an arrogant way, just it didn't even feel like a big deal. It was like, yeah, this is my track.

“I was an intense young human being. [There was a] certain period of time where I felt untouchable on those streets. I just felt like I was willing to take more risks and I was very happy to get my first pole, but I was nearly angry that I hadn't got it sooner. That's why I was like, now it's my time. I was running very high on confidence.

The F1 drivers who waited longest for a first pole position

“I couldn't do that today, but I can still take myself there and remember the feeling. I know why I was able to do it. Sometimes it does feel a little bit out of body. I think in those moments, maybe I was someone else.”

After beating Mercedes to the top spot around the Monte Carlo streets, he led the race in wet conditions and opted for a different strategy to Hamilton, switching from full wet tyres, to intermediates, and finally to slicks.

But when he peeled into the pits for his final stop, the Red Bull crew were equipped with the wrong compound, forcing Ricciardo to wait whilst they scrambled for the correct tyres. That allowed Hamilton to demote him to P2, and despite his best efforts to regain first place, he finished 7.252s behind the Briton.

“I left hardly anything on the table,” Ricciardo admitted. “There were certainly some years there that I didn't have that level of confidence and it went from being the best track for me to one of the worst, just like that.

“I think at the end of the day, what it was is they reacted to Lewis and what he did. I think they changed at the last second what to do. In simple terms, it's like they forgot the basics – control your controllables. I think there was panic and it was a mess. That was definitely one of my worst days in F1. I think if I never won Monaco after that, it would still hurt me a lot more.”

Redemption in Monaco

Two seasons later, Ricciardo took the Monaco win he deserved, albeit not in the most straightforward of ways. He had the advantage of starting from pole, but suffered a power loss for the majority of the 2018 event that made holding off Sebastian Vettel even more difficult.

“I had a very wounded car,” he explained. “At that moment, some of my lack of knowledge with the way Formula 1 cars work and how an engine works and those hybrid engines and all of this… I didn't really know what the problem was. I probably should have known, but if I knew, I think it would have made me realise how much worse it was.

“F1 cars have eight gears. In Monaco, because it's a shorter straight, you don't really even get to eight. So you're already just using seven gears. With that problem, I was only using six, so I had so much less power.

“I was telling the team and they were just giving me instructions like move your brakes forward or do this or do that. It was just problem solving. They weren't really giving me the script on what the problem was.”

While Ricciardo’s triumph overshadowed the painful memories from 2016 – and led to his iconic celebration in the Red Bull swimming pool – it came at the end of a day filled with anxiety and dread for the Australian.

He said: “I don't have 100 wins. I had eight, so they're all very special. But yes, more was on that than 2016. I think getting another chance to win Monaco made the pressure even higher.

“I just wanted it to be over. I wasn't looking forward to the race. I wasn't excited about anything. I was just like, I've hardly slept. Everyone's coming up to me, wishing me luck and trying to give me advice. I just want to go hide and get this race done and hopefully win and then go drink!

“The drivers that had won in Monaco that had raced with Red Bull had done flips into the pool. I was like, look, I'm probably going to embarrass myself. It's already been done. What's something that feels me? What feels kind of goofy? One of my favourite movies is Me, Myself and Irene. I love Jim Carrey.

“There's a scene where he leaps off a bridge and I feel like the way I did it, it was my memory of how he did it in that film. I was like, this will feel silly. I'm kind of laughing at myself doing a belly flop. A bit like the shoey, I didn't think it would be that cool at the time and it ended up being probably the most beautiful thing ever in F1!”

It became just as memorable as his shoey celebration, which involved drinking champagne out of his race boot to “show Australia that I'm proud to be Australian”. Other drivers and celebrities were convinced to join in, including Hamilton, Max Verstappen and acclaimed actor Sir Patrick Stewart.

“There was definitely a conscious part of it where the sport was still very serious,” Ricciardo described. “I would sometimes see drivers on the podium and they looked kind of miserable, and I couldn't really understand why. I get it if you lose the race on the last lap and you finish second instead of first, but there's just a lot of situations where I was like, the sport feels a little stiff.

“That was also my way of trying to bring in something else to the sport. It felt like the tie was choking everyone, and I was like, let's just undo a button here and relax a little. Then it just became my thing.

“I weirdly became relatable through doing the silly things. I realised it made it more fun for everyone else around me. Look, you have to get results to back it up. There was a time and place still, but I felt like the team appreciated it. I know it's serious and there's a lot of money and business involved in the sport, but we can still make it fun.”

Returning to glory with McLaren

Having left Red Bull in 2018, Ricciardo went on to race for Renault and McLaren, claiming his final race win with the latter at the 2021 Italian Grand Prix. After passing his former team mate Verstappen at the start, he beat Lando Norris to give the Woking-based outfit their first victory in nine years.

“I remember hearing the team in the background all celebrating and losing their minds, so that made me really happy,” he concluded. “When you succeed in the sport, everyone in the team feels a part of it. To celebrate it with such a big group of people, it's like a party.

“[It was] a year that I questioned myself a lot and lacked a lot of confidence – I hadn’t won in a few years, and I questioned, will I ever win again? That was a very real question. When it's been so long, you start having doubts as a team and as an organisation.

“For all of us to feel this sense of relief and like, oh my gosh, we do belong here. I knew it was our best chance of getting a podium that year, or my best chance, because I knew the car. We were quick on the straights, and Monza is very much a straight-line circuit.

Ranking Ricciardo’s 8 Grand Prix wins

“I always felt really good in Monza. It was a track I enjoyed, and I felt like myself again. I just had a certain mindset, which brought out a certain inner confidence. Was I thinking [I could] win? No, I was thinking a podium.

“It was my first win with another team, so that was also something I was personally proud of. Probably two months before that, I was very low, extremely low. I was proud of myself to be able to find it within me to pull it off.

“The opposite side of success can feel very lonely, but everyone played a part in winning on that day. Pit stop, strategy, reliability – it all just worked and everyone knows that they did their bit and they helped get that car to cross the line first. Celebrating with the team and seeing everyone smile as big as your own, that's very cool.”

title: Bruno Senna recounts Antonelli’s visit to his family farm
excerpt:
Bruno Senna – former F1 driver and nephew of three-time World Champion Ayrton Senna – has reflected on Kimi Antonelli’s trip to his family’s home, which saw the 20-year-old try out a karting track designed by the legendary Brazilian racer.

Shortly after securing his maiden Drivers’ Championship in Mexico City, Antonelli was invited to the Senna estate and got the chance to sit in the Lotus 98T, the car that Senna raced during the 1986 season.

He also met members of the family as he walked in the footsteps of his racing idol, whom he celebrated with a distinctive yellow and green tribute helmet at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

“We've known that he has been a super fan of Ayrton – and his dad as well, Marco – for a while, and I met him in Imola in 2024,” Senna explained on the latest episode of official podcast F1 Beyond The Grid.

“He was there and he was dressed from head to toe in Senna gear. He was doing Formula 2 there, and it was great to meet him. We had a nice chat. It's been so fun to have him be such a supporter.

“We got in touch with him and we offered the opportunity to come to the farm, and we knew that he would enjoy it. We took him around the farm. We took him into the little room where Ayrton did his aeroplane models, and he loved it.

“It was really, really fun to see him. We have the Lotus, the ‘86 car. We had him jump inside the car, and he didn't want to leave the car. You had the turbo boost knob, and he's exploring everything – having an anti-roll bar thing that you can change, and there's a gearstick.

“This is something that was quite funny – I was talking [about] next year when Lotus or McLaren want to do something, we can try to organise for [him] to drive one of these cars because he fits really well in the car.

“You know, his height is perfect for it. His dad was like, ‘I'm not sure if you can drive the manual car’, and Kimi was like, ‘sure I can!’. Finally, we drove on the go-kart track that Ayrton designed.

“It was a really fun thing when I was a kid, and Kimi was incredible. He was so fast, so consistent. We had a fun time. I would say that I was slower because I'm 10kg heavier, but I think there's a bit more than that in it, to be honest! He was amazing.

“The track was very dirty, very full of stone. Kimi was able to create a groove, and he was able to stay within that groove so consistently. It was really impressive. He couldn't move 10cm off because then you don't even run wide – you go onto the grass and spin out because it was so dirty. It was a really cool experience and showed why he's a World Champion.”

Over 30 years on from his untimely death at Imola, Senna is remembered as one of the greatest F1 drivers of all time and continues to motivate different generations – including his nephew, who raced in the sport between 2009 and 2011.

Thinking back to his personal experience on the grid, the younger Senna shared his admiration of Antonelli for maintaining his “humble” approach even whilst fighting for a title.

“When they landed, Marco came out of the helicopter and he had teary eyes because it was something that they never expected,” he said. “Marco was driving when he was younger, and I think he was able to instill this passion, this love for it in Kimi.

“But it also depends on the character of the child to take on this passion. I think Kimi – once he really understood what Ayrton represented as a human being, not only as a racing driver – got really inspired.

Who was Ayrton Senna and why is he regarded as one of F1’s greatest drivers?

“He's incredibly humble, incredibly down to earth. I think it's so easy for your mind to explode when you get into F1. This is a world where you're a god and everybody is [at] your feet, so it's so easy for you to just lose your track.

“I think that it's a difficult trait to be humble and have the right aggression, have the right attitude towards the sport at the same time. I think there are a lot of young drivers who are coming in with a really nice, very natural attitude into F1.

“Gabi [Bortoleto] has a really great heart, Ollie Bearman, Pierre [Gasly]. It makes me really proud of young kids who could be full of themselves, but they stay humble.

“I think this world is a very difficult world, very complicated. I've been here. I know how tricky it is to navigate this paddock, and to have people that are able to still be themselves throughout their F1 careers… For me, it's essential and very pleasing to see.”

title: Where do Mercedes rank among Teams' Championship winners
excerpt:
The Sao Paulo Grand Prix last weekend proved to be a day of celebration for Mercedes, as the German manufacturer secured the 2026 Constructors' Championship.

The Silver Arrows only needed a handful more points than Ferrari to secure the crown in Brazil, which moved Mercedes up to joint third in the all-time Constructors' Championship winners table.

But who remains ahead of them and which other teams have achieved the special accolade?

One-hit wonders

A total of 15 teams have won the Constructors' Championship since it was first introduced in 1958, with six of those managing to secure the title on only one occasion.

The very first was British manufacturer Vanwall during the inaugural season of the new championship standings, with three wins apiece for Stirling Moss and Tony Brooks as the team got the better of Ferrari before the end of the year.

Another British constructor also took the title in 1962, as Graham Hill took the first of his two drivers' titles with the BRM outfit, the combination securing four wins to edge out Jim Clark and Lotus to both titles.

Matra added their name to the list of winners in 1969, the French manufacturer supplying cars to Ken Tyrrell (before creating his own cars for 1970), with Jackie Stewart claiming the first of three drivers' titles.

Stewart's second title came in 1971, and with the help of Francois Cevert, Tyrrell was also able to claim the constructors' title under his own banner.

Nine wins for Michael Schumacher and a further two for team mate Johnny Herbert meant Benetton were able to beat Williams to the teams' crown in 1995, Schumacher also going back-to-back for the drivers' title before moving to Ferrari.

A member of the German's most trusted inner circle at Benetton and then the Scuderia would also add his name to the list of winning constructors, with Ross Brawn taking over Honda's entry for the 2009 season.

Jenson Button's six wins handed him the drivers' title, while two further victories for team mate Rubens Barrichello meant Brawn GP took the title, before morphing into Mercedes for 2010.

Back-to-back champions

Three teams in the history of F1 have only two Constructors' Championships to their name, and all three achieved the feat in back-to-back seasons.

Cooper became the first team, following in the wake of fellow British manufacturer Vanwall by winning the 1959 title with wins for that year's drivers' champion Jack Brabham, as well as Moss and Bruce McLaren.

Brabham secured the second of three drivers' titles the following year with five wins, while another victory for McLaren at the season-opener in Argentina helped Cooper retain their championship.

Having decided to design and build his own cars, in 1966 Brabham became the first, and so far only driver, to win the title racing a car bearing his own name, with the team securing both titles that season.

They achieved the same feat in 1967, but this time Brabham lost out on the drivers' title as team mate Denny Hulme took the accolade.

Despite coming close to title success in the early 1980s, it took until 2005 for Renault to reach the pinnacle of the sport, as Fernando Alonso ensured it was a double success.

The Spaniard and Renault squad, based out of Enstone and becoming what is now the Alpine team, won both titles again the following season in 2006, denying a resurgent Ferrari and Schumacher.

Red Bull (6 titles)

Having taken over the Jaguar outfit for the start of the 2005 season, Red Bull were generally seen by many as nothing more than an energy drinks company trying its hand at racing for a few years.

But under the leadership of Christian Horner and having acquired the services of design guru Adrian Newey from McLaren, the team began to make waves and claimed their first wins in 2009 as Sebastian Vettel and Mark Webber achieved six between them over the course of the campaign.

The duo then did enough to claim the team's first title the following season, with Vettel also winning the drivers' title in dramatic circumstances at an Abu Dhabi showdown.

That began a run of dominance as four double titles went the way of Red Bull and Vettel until the 2013 season, the team securing 41 wins with the German and Webber over that period.

New power unit changes for 2014 put Red Bull on the back foot, and despite occasional wins for Daniel Ricciardo and Max Verstappen, it wasn't until 2021 that the latter was able to have a title tilt for the first time.

Like Vettel, Verstappen went on a run of four consecutive titles, and with the help of team mate Sergio Perez, Red Bull also came away with two more titles in 2022 and 2023.

Lotus (7 titles)

Such was the dominance of Lotus under the leadership of team owner and designer Colin Chapman during the 1960s and 1970s, that the British manufacturer still remains fifth on this list.

Chapman's first title came in 1963 as he and Clark became one of the sport's greatest pairings, the Scot also taking that year's title as the combination did the double again in 1965.

Even Clark's death early in 1968 during an F2 race at Hockenheim couldn't prevent Chapman from another title double, this time with Hill taking his second drivers' title.

There was further tragedy just two years later, with Jochen Rindt securing the 1970 crown posthumously after his death in practice at Monza after five wins that season, with F1 rookie Emerson Fittipaldi winning in the US on just his fourth start to help secure the teams' title.

Fittipaldi would lead the team to the double again in 1972 at the wheel of the Lotus 72, with the Brazilian and team mate Ronnie Peterson claiming another crown for Lotus the following year, although both missed out on the drivers' title to Stewart.

Lotus and Chapman's final championship success came in 1978, the legendary designer creating the Lotus 79 with its ground effect aerodynamics, allowing Mario Andretti to also claim the drivers' title, although the success was overshadowed by the death of Peterson at Monza.

Although the team remained in F1 well into the 1990s even after Chapman's death in 1982, and achieved further victories with the likes of Elio de Angelis and Ayrton Senna, they never again claimed another title success.

Williams (9 titles)

Although Williams' last title came in 1997, they still remain joint third on the list.

The collaboration of team owner Frank Williams, designer Patrick Head and the no-nonsense approach of Alan Jones proved incredibly effective, and after wins in 1979, the first title followed in 1980 for both car and driver.

Although Jones and team mate Carlos Reutemann, missed out on the drivers' title the following season, the teams' title still went to Williams after the pair achieved two wins apiece.

Despite a drivers' title for Keke Rosberg in 1982, it took until 1986 for Williams to become the dominant force in F1 again with Honda engines, as they secured back-to-back teams' titles, along with the drivers' crown for Nelson Piquet in 1987.

Losing Honda power dropped the team down the pecking order, before a new collaboration with Renault brought their most prosperous period to date at the start of the 1990s.

Nigel Mansell finally secured his long-awaited title in 1992 as Williams dominated, with the team achieving both titles again in 1993 with Alain Prost leading the team.

Senna's death at the start of the 1994 season meant Damon Hill became Schumacher's main challenger, and although the Briton missed out on the individual crown, he along with Mansell and David Coulthard helped Williams secure another title.

Hill and Williams were finally on top in 1996, before Jacques Villeneuve secured the double again in 1997, which remains the team's final championship success to date.

Mercedes (9 titles)

Mercedes dominated F1 in 1955 with Juan Manuel Fangio and Stirling Moss, the former claiming that year's drivers' title, before the Silver Arrows left the sport for more than five decades.

Having taken over Brawn's outfit for the start of the 2010 season, it took until 2014 and an overhaul in power unit regulations before the team were back to winning ways.

But once they started winning, it was hard for the German manufacturer to stop as they claimed eight teams' titles between 2014 and 2021.

Those first three seasons saw Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg battle for the title, with the German finally claiming the sport's biggest prize in 2016 before retiring.

That opened the door for Valtteri Bottas to join the team, and although not as serious a title threat to Hamilton, the Finn ensured that Mercedes claimed another five teams' titles on the bounce, including in 2021 when Hamilton lost out on the drivers' title to Verstappen.

By that point Verstappen and Red Bull had become the dominant force in F1, and it took until another ruleset change at the beginning of 2026 for Mercedes to move back to the very front of the grid.

Kimi Antonelli became the youngest World Champion in F1 history at the Mexico City Grand Prix, while just a week later in Sao Paulo, Mercedes were once again back on top.

McLaren (10 wins)

Bruce McLaren's eponymous team continued even after his death during a testing accident at Goodwood in 1970, going on to become one of the most successful in F1.

The first of 10 teams' titles came in 1974, as Fittipaldi also claimed his second drivers' title, but it took another 10 years before McLaren had a driver combination to claim the constructors' accolade.

They found it in the shape of Niki Lauda and Prost, the pair separated by only half a point at the end of the 1984 season, before the latter went on a run of three consecutive titles – with McLaren claiming the teams' title in 1985.

With Senna joining McLaren for 1988, the combination became almost unbeatable as the team secured 15 out of 16 race wins that year, Senna just beating Prost to the title.

With Prost leaving for Ferrari, Senna and new team mate Gerhard Berger secured more titles across 1990 and 1991 before McLaren slipped down the pecking order.

It wasn't until 1998 when Mika Hakkinen, with the aid of Mercedes power, returned the team to the top after beating Schumacher and Ferrari, and although the Finn won again in 1999, McLaren missed out.

It took until 2024 for McLaren to reach the top again as a constructor, with Mercedes power once again helping Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri to victories, which culminated in the former winning the drivers' title in 2025 as McLaren defended their teams' crown.

Ferrari (16 titles)

Having been in F1 since the creation of the championship back in 1950, it's perhaps unsurprising that Ferrari should be top of this list.

The Scuderia got their first taste of title success as a manufacturer in 1961 as American Phil Hill won the drivers' title, which was followed three years later by another double, this time with John Surtees at the wheel.

Lauda's move in 1974 galvanised the team, and the following year they secured three teams' titles in succession with the Austrian also earning the drivers' crown in 1975 and 1977 – having returned from his fiery shunt and narrowly missing out in 1976.

Jody Scheckter and Gilles Villeneuve led the team to another brace of titles in 1979, the former claiming the drivers' title, before back-to-back team titles came in 1982 and 1983 as Didier Pironi, Rene Arnoux and Patrick Tambay all won races for the team.

It took until the late 1990s and Schumacher's influence to earn the Scuderia another title, which came in 1999 as a broken leg for the German opened the door for Eddie Irvine to challenge Hakkinen for the title.

Fully recovered for the start of the new decade, Schumacher and Ferrari became the dominant force in F1, claiming five consecutive drivers' and teams' titles.

With Schumacher retiring at the end of 2006, Kimi Raikkonen joined Felipe Massa at the team, the pair helping Ferrari to another title as the Finn ultimately claimed the drivers' title.

Although Massa just missed out on a drivers' title of his own to Hamilton the following season in the most dramatic circumstances, he and Raikkonen did enough to earn Ferrari a 16th title – currently the most recent it has achieved.

title: Bearman relieved ‘horrible three weeks’ for Haas are over
excerpt:
Ollie Bearman finished 17th in Sao Paulo last Sunday and afterwards cut a despondent figure as he revealed how pleased he was to be heading home after a tough triple header.

Bearman failed to finish the races in Austin and Mexico City, while his Sao Paulo Grand Prix unravelled thanks to some slow pit stops that dropped him from the fringes of the points to towards the back of the field.

Having put in a superb lap in the wet to qualify in the top 10, nothing in the Grand Prix quite went to plan for the Haas man, starting with early contact with Fernando Alonso that sent both drivers wide after a handful of corners.

“I had a bit of a moment at the start but nothing major, I lost a few places at the start but managed to gain back a few again, so was net zero,” he explained. “After that I just had some very slow pit stops and I couldn’t fight with that.”

That pit stop dropped him from P10 to P17 on a day where points felt possible, with the rain causing havoc and plenty of strategic dilemmas to contend with. Anyone who got those strategy calls right could have climbed up the order – as shown by Nico Hulkenberg managing to finish P10 despite serving a 10-second time penalty.

“I just want to go home and reset. It has been a horrible three weeks, we have missed two opportunities to score points, and we just need to move on and do better,” Bearman concluded.

His triple header started with problems in Austin when he made contact with Pierre Gasly when fighting for position. That earned him a 10-second time penalty for causing a collision, which combined with the resultant damage forced his retirement.

“I sent one up the inside, and to be honest, he saw me as he left space but to me, it didn’t feel enough. He gave space, but only half a car's worth, and I was committed, so we made a bit of contact – I picked up a huge amount of damage on my car, and I probably damaged his car as well,” was what Bearman said at the time.

Camara experiences every condition in 'tricky' Haas debut

"It was a shame as I felt like I was massively penalised anyway, as the damage ruined my race, and on top of that I picked up the penalty. In my view, it was a racing incident.”

Worse was to come in Mexico City, when he was hit from behind by Hulkenberg, forcing another retirement with damage.

On a day where so many post-race penalties were handed out, Bearman lost the opportunity to score – with his stand-in team mate Ryo Hirakawa promoted to P10 from his 13th place finish.

“I just got smashed off. I was turning into Turn 4, and the next thing I knew, I was looking at everyone else coming past me, facing the wrong way,” Bearman said of the moment.

“It was a good race to be honest, I had great pace, and we were in the fight for points, and I was in the points when I was taken out. It happens, it just sucks.”

As a result of all that, it is easy to see why Bearman is keen to go home, with Haas scoring just the one point in the last three-race run, while rivals Audi managed to pick up five points to close the gap in the standings in the fight for seventh.

Haas remain in front, but only by three points with three rounds remaining.

title: Daniel Ricciardo explains 'shoey' origin: 'I felt like a tie was choking everyone'
excerpt:
Daniel Ricciardo has revealed that the celebration that came to define his F1 career began as a message to friends back home in Australia rather than a calculated stunt.

Ricciardo, who retired from Formula 1 after the 2024 Singapore Grand Prix following 257 starts, eight wins and 32 podiums across a 14-year career, has reflected on the gesture that followed him from Red Bull to Renault, and onto McLaren.

Ricciardo said the act began on the podium after the 2016 German Grand Prix, in which he was second, long before it became an expected ritual whenever he finished on the rostrum.

"I did it really for my friends watching back home, and I knew that they'd text me after being like, 'You're a legend. You did it for Australia'," said Ricciardo. "[I was a] Bit of a bogan, someone who doesn't take themselves so seriously, I guess.

"And there were some friends and a group of guys in Australia who were doing a lot of it, and they had quite a big presence on social media and stuff.

"So it was becoming like Australia, or a part of Australia, was owning it a little bit, and then there were some Australian sports people and celebrities and that who were doing it.

"So I was like, 'Okay, I want to be a part of this and show Australia that I'm proud to be Australian."

[Article continues below]

Riccaiardo - 'Let's undo a button'

Ricciardo explained that beyond the Australian pride angle, he also wanted to loosen up a paddock he found overly formal, even in victory.

"There was definitely a conscious part of it, where the sport was still very serious," he said. "I would see drivers on the podium sometimes, and they looked miserable, and I couldn't really understand why.

"I get it if you lose the race on the last lap and you finish second instead of first.

"But there were a lot of situations where I was like, the sport feels a little stiff, and that was also my way of trying to bring in something else to the sport. I felt like the tie was choking everyone, and I was like, 'Let's undo a button here and relax a little'.

"And then it just became my thing, and it wasn't really planned to have been something that I would have done again."

It became such an iconic moment on the podium that others followed suit, not least the late renowned actor Sir Patrick Stewart after the 2017 Canadian GP.

"I hadn't even got to the point of asking him if he wanted to do it yet," said Ricciardo. "He asked me if he could do it, so he basically demanded it, and I was like, 'This is very cool', so I knew it had caught some wind by that point."

Even seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton got in on the act, after previously stating that, "The juice from the foot is not something I wish to drink."

Ricciardo said: "Lewis was also quoted saying once he'd never do it, and then he did.

"I'm just glad it was always my shoe. I gave the people what they wanted."

title: Alan Jones remembered for 'indelible mark' in touching Williams family tribute
excerpt:
Alan Jones left an "indelible mark" on the history of the Williams F1 team, believes former boss Claire Williams.

Jones, the 1980 F1 world champion, died last week aged 80 after a short illness in Australia.

The 12-time grand prix winner entered the history books in 1980 as the first driver to win the world title for Williams, with the likes of Nelson Piquet, Nigel Mansell, and Alain Prost following in his footsteps for Sir Frank Williams and Sir Patrick Head.

Jones was often used as the yardstick by which all Williams drivers were judged, having raced for the team between 1978 and 1981, with former deputy team principal and Sir Frank's daughter, Claire, reflecting on the Melbourne native's passing.

"It was so sad to hear of Alan's passing," Williams told RacingNews365 exclusively.

"There are a number of people who have been a part of the team over a long, long period of our history, and there have been a good handful that have left such an indelible mark as Alan did.

"He was Dad and Patrick's first world champion, and that meant an enormous amount. I was very young; I was only four when Alan raced for us, but I knew him and built a lovely relationship with him when I was team principal, and he was enormously supportive of me, courtesy of his relationship with my dad.

"He wasn't a driver that came and went as much as his time in the sport was pretty short comparatively. He just had a personality that my dad truly admired and respected, and I think they were very similar in their personalities.

"It was that just kind of mindset of roll your sleeves up, put in every ounce of your fibre to get the job done and to win. That was their mindset.

"Unfortunately, it's another racing great [who has died]. It's another icon who is no longer here, and that's incredibly sad.

"My thoughts are with his family, with his friends, and those who will feel his passing sorely."

title: Liam Lawson closing in on century in tight race to beat all-time F1 record
excerpt:
Now Liam Lawson has secured his place on the 2027 grid with Racing Bulls, the New Zealander can turn his attention to beating an all-time team record.

Racing Bulls put an end to weeks of speculation on Thursday with the announcement that Lawson and Arvid Lindblad would form the team's 2027 driver pairing, with Nikola Tsolov having to wait longer to make his bow.

For Lawson, with his future now secure, he can fully turn his sights to beating a team record, set in a former guise.

As of the Sao Paulo GP, and his seventh-place finish, Lawson has a total of 89 points to his name - 21 behind Gasly with three races remaining.

However, it must be caveated that 14 of Lawson's points were scored for Red Bull in the Dutch and Spanish GPs as he deputised for the injured Isack Hadjar.

title: Isack Hadjar expresses sadness at all-too-soon F1 season ending
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has expressed his sadness that the F1 season is on the cusp of ending, declaring that he still feels like he has "a lot in the tank."

In his first season at Red Bull, Hadjar has performed well, scooping three podiums in support of Max Verstappen, but missed the Dutch, Italian, and Spanish Grands Prix after sustaining a wrist injury during the summer break, meaning he did not race between the Hungarian GP on July 26th and the Azerbaijan GP on September 26th.

This two-month lay-off came after no grands prix were held in April, with the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian races unable to be held as scheduled due to the Iran War, with one race in the two months between the Japanese GP on March 29th and the Canadian GP on May 26th.

Although F1 has signalled that the Qatar and Abu Dhabi races will go ahead to finish the season with Imola formally stood down as a replacement venue, there is a slim possibility that the upcoming Las Vegas GP could still be the end of the campaign if tensions in the Middle East re-escalate.

Reflecting on whether his injury lay-off had disrupted his momentum, Hadjar rejected the idea.

"No, because I got very lucky with the timing because the three races I skipped, I remember, were a bit tricky," Hadjar told media, including RacingNews365.

"I definitely came back when the car made the step. At the same time, I feel like this year, for some reason, I feel like I haven't driven much.

"Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were cancelled, and then I had a two-month break during the summer, and now I feel like I have a lot left in the tank, and considering what's happening in the coming races and we don't know how many more races we are going to have, I'm a bit sad that we're already at the end.

"I feel like I can still go a long way this year."

[Article continues below]

Red Bull's step forward

Since Hadjar returned to Baku, the team has enjoyed a strong run of form, with Verstappen winning three races in Bahrain, Malaysia, Singapore, and Mexico City, as well as the Singapore Sprint.

Hadjar has taken podiums in Baku and Sao Paulo in addition to his one earlier in the season in Monaco, just as the RB22 has taken a dramatic upturn in performance - something he says gives him hope for 2027.

"But I'm proud of the guys for the big step [we made]," he said.

"In Melbourne we were second off the pace; at round three [in Japan], we were a second off. Now the car is winning races and fighting for podiums, so I can't be more proud of that.

"The way we developed the car, the ability of the team to progress quickly [makes me] very hopeful for next year."

title: FIA set hearing date with F1-comeback hero's result at risk
excerpt:
The FIA has confirmed Audi's appeal date for the case against the final result of the Italian Grand Prix after the German team took issue with the outcome of a post-race investigation into Yuki Tsunoda.

In early September, Tsunoda ended the race at Monza in P10 to score his first point of the year whilst deputising for Liam Lawson at Racing Bulls.

He avoided a penalty after being investigated by the stewards, having been flagged for a potential starting infringement.

Tsunoda originally lined up on the wrong side of the grid at a red flag restart following an incident involving Charles Leclerc, but moved to correct it; however, he found himself positioned at an awkward angle in his grid box.

Race control opted to call an aborted start, and under Article B5.9.4 of the sporting regulations, it stipulates that any driver who causes an extra formation lap must be moved to the pit lane.

However, the stewards determined that it was the race director, rather than Tsunoda, who instigated the extra lap.

After Gabriel Bortoleto finished behind Tsunoda in the race and just outside of the points, Audi appealed the stewards' decision.

The case will now be heard by the International Court of Appeal at 09:00 local time in Paris, on 25th November, 2026.

title: Why Max Verstappen was 'high-profile victim' of Red Bull 'phenomenon' in Brazil
excerpt:
A phenomenon, one that had arguably never manifested itself as clearly as it did for Red Bull during the São Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday, involved the tyres intermittently falling outside their optimal operating temperature window.

At Interlagos, Max Verstappen was a high-profile victim of this issue. After starting from 21st on the grid, and after a sensational first stint on intermediate tyres, he reported a sudden drop in his car's overall performance after switching to softs, noting, in particular, that its behaviour had become more unstable and less consistent.

In essence, it was as if the RB22 had begun to exhibit problems that had seemingly been left behind earlier in the season: instability mid-corner, primarily at the rear, along with noticeable understeer upon corner entry and distinct oversteer on exit through the track’s more twisty sections.

The frequent 'snaps' from the rear end indicated that the available tyre grip was vanishing, not due to standing water, but because of a loss of aerodynamic downforce caused by an unstable car platform.

In part, this was a byproduct of the setups chosen for Interlagos; due to adverse weather conditions, the cars were run at a higher ride height, which significantly reduced the downforce generated by the floor and shifted the centre of pressure forward, thereby lightening the rear end.

Consequently, the RB22 found itself in a situation where the developments that had previously ensured a consistent balance between its dynamic and aerodynamic behaviour were no longer effective.

As track temperatures fluctuated and, crucially, as the car became lighter throughout the race, tyre degradation triggered sharp, sudden shifts in the vehicle's handling, leaving Verstappen to contend with a high degree of unpredictability.

It is therefore reasonable to argue that the conditions encountered in Brazil, with a track surface that kept changing its grip level in an inconsistent manner, led the drivers, and Verstappen in particular, to perceive the car’s handling as less precise.

This deprived him of the confidence needed to push to the limit and extract the remaining performance from the car, precisely what would have been required to contend for the win.

title: Red Bull map out clear F1 2028 route for 'exceptional talent'
excerpt:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has clearly indicated that Nikola Tsolov will be on the F1 grid in 2028.

The announcement comes after Racing Bulls confirmed on Wednesday that Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will remain its race line-up for 2027, closing off the only seat available for Tsolov in the short term.

Instead, the 19-year-old Bulgarian will spend next year on an extensive programme combining simulator work, Testing of Previous Cars outings and mandatory rookie first practice sessions, a pathway Red Bull has previously used to prepare its juniors.

Tsolov, who moved from the Alpine Academy into the Red Bull junior setup for 2025, is currently fighting for the Formula 2 title in his first full season at that level.

Mekies has made clear that the timeline for 2027 is explicitly about preparation rather than competition.

"Nikola is an exceptionally talented young driver, and we have been hugely impressed by his development and performances over the past few years," said Mekies.

"To fight for the championship in F3 and now challenge for the F2 title in his first full season says a great deal about his ability and determination.

"What has impressed us just as much is his maturity, his approach to racing and his willingness to keep learning and improving.

"We have enormous belief in Nikola's potential and see him as a driver with a very exciting future in F1.

"This appointment reflects our confidence in him and our commitment to his continued development. Our focus in 2027 will be on giving him the experience, tools and support he needs to be ready to race in F1 next.

"For now, Nikola still has an important job to finish in F2. We wish him every success in the final two rounds and will be supporting him all the way as he fights for the championship."

[Article continues below]

Tsolov - 'My ambition is clear'

Tsolov himself has framed his upcoming reserve role as the final step before reaching the grid.

Expressing his obvious delight with his position for next year, Tsolov added: "Since joining the junior team, I've received amazing support and have developed so much, both as a driver and as a person.

"My career has progressed incredibly quickly, and I owe a lot to everyone who has believed in me and helped me get to this point.

"My ambition is clear: I want to become an F1 driver. Having the opportunity to spend next year preparing for that next step is incredibly exciting.

"I'm confident that with the team's support and experience, I'll have the best possible preparation to make sure I'm fully ready to take the next step onto the F1 grid when the time comes.

"I know there is still a lot to learn, but I'm ready to work hard, make the most of every opportunity and give everything I have to the team.

"For now, my immediate focus is on finishing the F2 season as strongly as possible."

title: Red Bull confirm third driver for 2027 after Liam Lawson-Arvid Lindblad decision
excerpt:
Red Bull and Racing Bulls have confirmed F2 title-chaser Nikola Tsolov as its third driver for the 2027 season.

Tsolov will be on hand at every grand prix weekend next year while continuing to build toward a likely race seat with the team in 2028.

The announcement comes after the Faenza-based squad confirmed that Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will keep their race seats for next year, leaving no immediate cockpit available for the Red Bull junior.

Instead, Tsolov will be given a heavy Testing of Previous Cars programme, running older-specification machinery to accumulate mileage.

Tsolov was given his first taste of grand prix machinery this year with a TPC run-out at Imola followed by a first practice outing in Mexico.

That involvement will expand significantly in 2027, with the 19-year-old set to take multiple FP1 sessions across the year under the FIA's rule requiring teams to field young drivers who have not started more than two grands prix.

Red Bull confirmed that, "In his new role, Nikola will undertake an extensive development programme, combining simulator and development work with valuable track experience through free practice sessions, Testing of Previous Cars (TPC), selected test sessions and tyre testing.

"Alongside his responsibilities as a reserve driver, the programme is designed to ensure he is fully prepared to race in F1 at the highest level."

Tsolov, who is managed by Fernando Alonso's A14 Management agency, rose through Spanish F4 with Campos Racing before progressing through F3 and into F2. He left the Alpine Academy in late 2024 before being picked up by the Red Bull junior programme ahead of the 2025 season.

With no race seat opening up for next year, Red Bull had been weighing alternative options to keep Tsolov active. Speculation indicated a switch to DTM had been considered. That route has been shelved in favour of the expanded Racing Bulls role.

title: Shock feat achieved not even Verstappen or Hamilton have managed – On This Day
excerpt:
On this day 31 years ago, an F1 record was broken!

Thirty-one years ago today, Damon Hill produced a victory at the Australian Grand Prix in Adelaide that has never been matched since.

The Williams driver won by two full laps over second-placed Olivier Panis, a feat that remains the most recent occasion in Formula 1 history where the race winner lapped every other finisher in the field.

Hill started from pole and led every one of the 81 laps, crossing the line in a time of 1:49:15.946 with no serious challenge to his supremacy.

The scale of the margin was extraordinary even by the standards of the era, and it has stood as a statistical outlier, with no winner in the three decades since managing to put the entire field a lap down.

The result carried no championship weight. Michael Schumacher had already wrapped up both the drivers' and constructors' titles for Benetton two rounds earlier at the Pacific Grand Prix, meaning Hill's win in Adelaide was pure redemption rather than title business.

After a campaign littered with errors and high-profile clashes with Schumacher, the victory offered Hill a measure of personal momentum heading into the off-season and eased some of the media scrutiny that had built up around him.

Driver

Damon Hill

British

Chaos behind triggers staggering winning margin

The race itself was chaotic behind Hill. David Coulthard, Hill's Williams team-mate, had been leading before sliding into the pit wall on lap 20 after carrying too much speed into the pit entry.

Roberto Moreno repeated the exact same mistake two laps later, crashing into the same stretch of concrete.

Schumacher and Jean Alesi then collided on lap 23 fighting over position through turn three, damage to the Ferrari's front wing and the Benetton's suspension ending both their afternoons.

The weekend had already been overshadowed by a frightening qualifying accident involving Mika Häkkinen, whose McLaren crashed into the barriers at Brewery Bend after a tyre deflation.

The Finn required an emergency roadside tracheotomy from circuit medical staff, a moment that underlined how perilous the sport remained even as Hill's afternoon in the race itself unfolded without drama.

With so many rivals eliminated and the lapped traffic stacking up behind him, Hill cruised home untroubled, closing out a season of personal struggle with the kind of dominant display that, three decades on, still stands alone in the record books.

title: George Russell clears Mercedes of blame after F1 title dream disaster
excerpt:
George Russell has emphatically rejected the idea that Mercedes has 'let him down' following his 2026 F1 title defeat to Kimi Antonelli.

Russell entered the first season of F1's new technical regulations as the overwhelming favourite to be crowned world champion, and underlined this status in the opening round of the season by winning the Australian Grand Prix from pole position.

He then started the Chinese GP weekend strongly by winning the Sprint, before a battery issue stopped him on track in Q3, limiting him to one run as Antonelli swept to pole.

The Italian then converted into a first grand prix victory, as he then unleashed five straight victories, including in Canada, where Russell, who had won the Sprint, retired from the lead with an engine failure.

In Britain and Belgium, there was a deployment issue on his car, which then struck again on race-day at Spa on the opening lap, leaving him vulnerable to attack from behind, as he collided with Lewis Hamilton at Les Combes and retired as Antonelli won.

Then, when fighting for a podium in Bahrain and Malaysia, he suffered yet another power unit failure before another deployment issue struck on the long run from the start to Turn 1 in Mexico City on the opening lap, dropping him from second on the grid to sixth at Turn 1, as he then collided with Isack Hadjar and earned a 10-second time penalty.

Antonelli sealed the title after that race, with Russell leaving the circuit before even speaking to media, something Mercedes was fined €5,000 for.

Reflecting, the Briton believes that the team has not let him down and his poor season is simply part and parcel of grand prix racing.

"I don't think the team have let me down, honestly, because these things do happen," Russell told media, including RacingNews365.

"Nobody intends for it to happen. We're all trying our best to deliver the best, and last year we had an extremely reliable car, and you know we only finished fourth in the championship.

"This year, we have a car that's extremely fast, but has been unreliable. So, which one do you prefer?

"We weren't satisfied last year, and then of course, even though the team will win both championships, they're still not satisfied with this season.

"And then, as for my own championship, it's difficult to put a number on how much it's impacted the championship because it's often about momentum.

"When we started the season, we had the issue in China with the failure in qualifying. We had the issues in Japan. We had the engine failure in Canada and the drive-through penalty that wasn't a drive-through penalty in Monaco. These things compound."

[Article continues below]

Was Russell overdriving?

Russell then added that another factor in his struggles could possibly lay in the fact that after his setbacks, he was trying to "overachieve" with his driving to ensure Antonelli did not get too far ahead in the points table.

"If you're in the championship fight or you're within touching distance, you feel like you're having to catch up [after the setbacks]", he added

"And maybe that contributed towards overdriving and trying to overachieve. Maybe not.

"You can't answer it, and I'm not looking to answer it. Just, altogether, it just hasn't been the year I wanted."

title: Lewis Hamilton makes heartfelt visit in between grands prix: ‘It’s an injustice'
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has visited the Rafah border crossing near the Gaza Strip to witness efforts to transport aid and supplies into Gaza.

Rafah is the only crossing point Palestine shares with another country that is not Israel, with Hamilton visiting the Egyptian side of the border where food, medical, and clothing supplies are being prepared to be delivered to those inside the Strip.

A ceasefire agreement reached in 2025 between Palestine and Israel put a stop to major combat operations, but an agreement of 600 trucks of aid per day has thus far not been reached.

After his tour of the aid facilities, Hamilton took to social media to explain that one truck driver he spoke to had been waiting for "over 12 hours" to enter the Strip - with crossings denied for "crazy reasons" as he called Israel's actions in Gaza "appalling" and said it was "an injustice for people to be denied their freedom, their safety, and their dignity."

"The past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling," he wrote on social media.

"It’s an injustice for people to be denied their freedom, their safety and their dignity. No human being should be treated as though their life matters less.

"I saw walls stretching for miles, built to keep them in. Standing there, outside what felt like an open-air prison, all I could think about was getting in to help.

"At [the] Rafah border, I saw food trucks lined up ready to go, but they’re regularly not allowed in or face major delays. The first driver in line that I spoke to had already been waiting over 12 hours.

"At the nearby logistics centre, I saw the hard work of the aid workers, but I also saw what gets rejected for crazy reasons. Sleeping bags, first aid kits, medical equipment, wheelchairs, even footballs for kids.

"Israel needs to fulfil its obligations under the ceasefire and let the aid trucks in. No excuse.

"I know so many people feel that same helplessness. That same need to do something rather than just watch. I don’t want us to get used to their suffering. I don’t want us to look away."

title: Former Red Bull junior completes Lola 2027 Formula E driver line-up
excerpt:
Lola Formula E has completed its rookie line-up for the 2027 season, confirming Enzo Fittipaldi alongside Robert Shwartzman.

It will be the Brazilian's first season in the all-electric championship. Fittipaldi previously took part in the rookie test in Berlin in 2024.

A former Italian F4 champion and FRECA runner-up, Fittipaldi worked his way up through the single-seater ladder, racing in both Formula 3 and Formula 2. He took two wins and 13 podiums during his time in F2. He was also a Red Bull junior in 2023.

The 25-year-old then switched to INDY NXT this year, finishing runner-up in the championship with four wins, more than any other driver on the grid.

Fittipaldi has already been putting in laps in the Lola T004, working closely with Lola and technical partner Yamaha, which continues to supply engineering expertise and innovation for the GEN4 powertrain.

Fittipaldi said he was relishing the opportunity to join the Silverstone-based manufacturer for his Formula E bow.

"I'm extremely excited to be joining Lola for my debut season in Formula E," said Fittipaldi.

"This is a big step forward in my racing career, and I'm incredibly grateful to the team for putting their trust in me and giving me this opportunity.

"Lola is a name with so much history and heritage in motorsport, and it's a privilege to be part of this new chapter alongside Yamaha. I'm also thrilled to be joining the team at such an exciting time, with projects like the T70S bringing Lola's iconic past into the future.

"I can't wait to get behind the wheel for [the] upcoming test in Madrid, start working closely with the team, and build towards a strong first season together."

[Article continues below]

Fittipaldi 'a great fit' for Lola

Team principal Mark Preston said Fittipaldi's background across multiple single-seater categories would stand him in good stead for the switch to electric machinery.

"Enzo is a great fit for Lola Formula E, bringing experience from a range of single-seater series that will prove beneficial as he transitions to all-electric racing," said Preston.

"He has the talent, work ethic and technical understanding to be a great asset as we enter this new era for the sport and during testing he has shown a strong ability to work effectively alongside the engineers to help us extract as much performance as possible from the T004."

Fittipaldi's arrival at Lola extends a multi-generational link between the manufacturer and his family.

In 1970, his grandfather Emerson Fittipaldi and great-uncle Wilson went head-to-head in the Brazilian Sportscar Championship, driving a Lola T210 and T70 Mk3B respectively.

Emerson later returned to the marque in 1988, emerging as a title contender in the CART PPG IndyCar World Series at the wheel of a T87/00.

Wilson's son Christian went on to score 12 CART IndyCar podiums for Newman-Haas Racing in Lola machinery, including a win at the 2000 season finale at Fontana Speedway, and also represented Brazil in the final four rounds of the inaugural A1 GP series, driving a Lola B05/52 in 2006.
